page_contents_html:
Background

Male hypogonadism requires both symptoms and biochemical testosterone deficiency; neither alone is sufficient to diagnose it or to refer. Typical symptoms are reduced libido, erectile dysfunction, and loss of spontaneous or early-morning erections. Some men instead present with a low-impact (osteoporotic) fracture or an unexplained normocytic anaemia.

Testosterone <7 nmol/L more often reflects a secondary (gonadal or pituitary) cause; 7–11 nmol/L more often reflects non-gonadal illness or late-onset hypogonadism associated with increasing age and obesity.

accordion_sections.heading: Assessment
accordion_sections.html:
Do not test during an acute, reversible illness or when symptoms are vague — testosterone falls transiently and the result will mislead. Test when the patient is well.

First test — total testosterone. Brown tube, taken 0800–0900h; reference range 10–30 nmol/L. Interpret against three bands:

<7 nmol/L — androgen deficiency likely

7–11 nmol/L — equivocal

>11 nmol/L — androgen deficiency unlikely. Referral not indicated; consider another cause for the symptoms.

For a result <7 or 7–11 nmol/L with no co-existing illness, repeat in 4 weeks — fasted, 0800–0900h — with bioavailable testosterone, LH/FSH, prolactin, TSH and ferritin. The confirmatory panel is the same for both bands; only the subsequent action differs (see Who to refer).

accordion_sections.heading: Primary care management
accordion_sections.html:
Complete these steps before referring; each may resolve the low result or remove the need for referral.

  • Confirm the diagnosis. A single low reading is not diagnostic — repeat fasted at 0800–0900h with the confirmatory panel (bioavailable testosterone, LH/FSH, prolactin, TSH, ferritin).
  • Review medication for drugs that cause androgen deficiency (see below).
  • Address lifestyle and weight. In milder deficiency, a 5–10% weight loss may improve testosterone concentrations.

Drugs that cause androgen deficiency

  • Opiates, including methadone (and illicit opiates)
  • Glucocorticoids — particularly high-dose oral or parenteral
  • Anabolic or gonadal steroids
  • Alkylating / antineoplastic (chemotherapy) agents — current or recent
  • Drugs causing hyperprolactinaemia — antipsychotics, anti-emetics, some antidepressants
  • Alcohol excess and drugs of abuse (e.g. cannabis, amphetamines)
  • Anticonvulsants — carbamazepine and phenobarbitone
  • Others — e.g. ketoconazole, spironolactone

Chemotherapy, opiate and anabolic-steroid effects can be profound and may persist long after the drug is stopped.

accordion_sections.heading: Who to refer
accordion_sections.html:
Refer to endocrinology

  • Confirmed testosterone <7 nmol/L — once illness and drug effects are excluded.
  • Confirmed 7–11 nmol/L — only where the patient is clearly symptomatic, not improving, and illness/drug effects are excluded.

Endocrinology accepts referrals for confirmed testosterone deficiency and will discuss treatment. In borderline cases a 3–6 month therapeutic trial may be considered after counselling on the potential benefits and risks.

accordion_sections.heading: Who not to refer
accordion_sections.html:
• Testosterone >11 nmol/L — androgen deficiency unlikely.
  • An unconfirmed single low reading — repeat and complete the panel first.
  • Any low result taken during acute illness or with vague symptoms — repeat when the patient is well.
  • Confirmed 7–11 nmol/L who are asymptomatic or improving — repeat in 6 months if symptoms persist.

accordion_sections.heading: Treatment and shared-care monitoring
accordion_sections.html:
Treatment is initiated and titrated by endocrinology, which monitors for the first year and, if stable, discharges to primary care for ongoing annual monitoring. This section supports GPs continuing established treatment.

Absolute contraindications to testosterone treatment

  • Desire for fertility — fertility services guide treatment instead
  • Current prostate carcinoma
  • Breast carcinoma
  • Haematocrit >0.50
  • Unevaluated elevated PSA or prostate lump on digital rectal examination
  • NYHA grade 3 or 4 heart failure
  • Liver tumour
  • Hypercalcaemia
  • Nephrotic syndrome

Monitoring

  • Check FBC, PSA, lipids and LFTs before starting.
  • PSA at baseline then annually; bone density at baseline then every 4 years.
  • Repeat monitoring at 3, 6 and 12 months, then annually.
  • Monitor the haematocrit to avoid polycythaemia.
  • In milder deficiency from non-gonadal illness, consider stopping at 3–6 months if there is no clinical improvement.

Counselling points: long-term cardiovascular safety is unknown; testosterone does not cause prostate cancer but may promote growth of an existing tumour; BPH symptoms may be unmasked; some studies report increased risk of venous thromboembolism, atrial fibrillation and fractures; and erectile dysfunction may not improve. Routine prostate cancer screening during treatment is not recommended, though a baseline PSA monitored annually is usual practice.

Preparations — base the choice of gel or injection on patient preference and availability; gels are often used first to assess response and tolerability.

  • Tostran 2% gel (10 mg per metered application; abdomen or inner thighs) — usual maintenance 4 applications (40 mg) once daily; max 8 applications (80 mg) daily.
  • Testogel 16.2 mg/g sachet (40.5 mg per 2.5 g sachet; upper arms/shoulders) — usual 1 sachet (40.5 mg) once daily; max 2 sachets (81 mg) daily.
  • Testogel 16.2 mg/g pump (20.25 mg per actuation; upper arms/shoulders) — usual 2 actuations (40.5 mg) once daily; max 4 actuations (81 mg) daily.
  • Nebido (testosterone undecanoate) 1 g/4 mL deep IM — first two injections 6 weeks apart, then every 10–14 weeks, aiming for a trough at or just below the lower reference limit before the third injection.
  • Sustanon 250 mg IM — usually 1 mL every 3 weeks. Contains arachis oil — contraindicated in peanut or soya allergy.

Gels: apply to clean, dry skin (not the genital area), wash hands afterwards, and avoid skin-to-skin contact for about 6 hours. Check testosterone 2–6 hours after the morning application, aiming for the middle of the reference range; a level >30 nmol/L requires a dose reduction (consider sample contamination).
